headline_insight: Value-added service uptake is effectively zero across the sample: fewer than 0.5% of both women and men report having used any of the teleconsultation, face-to-face consultation, medicine-discount, lab-test or mobile-clinic benefits, with literally no lab test use recorded among 2,104 respondents.
paragraphs: The most striking finding in this section is an absence rather than a gap. Across 1,518 female and 586 male respondents, uptake of every listed value-added benefit sits at or near zero. Teleconsultation (phone doctor) was used by four women (0.3%) and no men; face-to-face consultations by four women (0.3%) and one man (0.2%); access to discounted or free medicines by a single female client (0.1%); health events such as mobile clinics, ambulances or health brigades by one male client (0.2%); and lab examinations by nobody at all. None of these differences are statistically significant after adjustment \.3 percentage points or less in every case \ and it would be a mistake to read them as gendered patterns. The gender story here is that women and men are equally disconnected from the ancillary benefits attached to their cover. Benchmark data is not available for this indicator, so we cannot say how this uptake compares to industry or peer-portfolio norms.

The small group of clients who answered the claim-services follow-up question offers a tentative counterpoint, but the base is far too small to carry weight: of seven women, three (42.9%) found claim-related services very helpful and two (28.6%) somewhat helpful, while both of the two men who answered placed themselves in the neutral "neither helpful nor unhelpful" category. This subgroup is flagged n_ok=false and should be treated as illustrative only \ a headline 85.7-point gender difference resting on nine respondents in total is a description of nine people, not of the portfolio. What it does hint at, directionally, is that where clients do engage with a service, the experience is not negative; the binding constraint appears to be contact, not quality.

The open-text responses reinforce that reading, and are revealing in what clients name as the "additional service" they actually received. A male client in Uganda described being "taught the group how to pay money for vision fund," while male clients in Kenya named "Trainings" and "Table banking." None of these are health benefits. Clients are describing group-based financial and operational support \ the things they visibly experience through the group channel \ rather than the teleconsultation, medicine or diagnostic benefits the product formally offers. This suggests the health-adjacent services are either not embedded in the client journey, not communicated at the point of enrolment or renewal, or not reachable in practice.

For programming and product design, the implication is that these benefits are currently close to notional. Before investing further in expanding the service bundle, VisionFund should establish whether the near-zero uptake reflects an awareness failure, an access failure (network coverage, provider proximity, phone ownership and airtime, which general sector context suggests fall disproportionately on women and clients with disabilities), or benefits that are simply not operational in some markets. A practical next step is to test awareness directly \ asking clients whether they know each benefit exists \ and to route benefit communication through the group meeting and repayment touchpoints that clients themselves already identify as where they receive support. Given that uptake is uniformly low rather than gender-skewed, the immediate priority is universal activation rather than a gender-targeted intervention, though any activation design should be tested for whether it reaches women and clients with disabilities on equal terms.
